Lessons.Title: Representing Situations with Inequalities
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: translate contextual minimum, maximum, exactly and strict constraints into inequalities, define a variable with units and justify feasible values. Edulytiks original adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U02:L18, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/18/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Building On 6.EE.B.5 and 7.EE.B.4; Addressing HSA-CED.A.3; Building Towards HSA-CED.A.3 and HSN-Q.A.2.

Original community workshop scenario: a venue has a fixed $20 reservation cost and $7 supplies per registered participant. Total budget is at most $100, so 20+7n≤100. Because n counts people, n must be a nonnegative integer. At least 6 participants must register: n≥6. Combining these gives n=6,7,8,9,10 or 11. If 12 attend, total is $104 and exceeds budget.

Discuss language differences: 'at most' includes equality (≤), 'under' excludes equality (<), 'at least' includes equality (≥) and 'more than' excludes equality (>). Constraints also include physical maximum occupancy and nonnegative count domains even if they were not stated in the expense formula.

Student task: invent two plausible workshop modifications, represent each with multiple inequalities and test boundary cases that distinguish strict and inclusive limits. Partner critique should catch missing units and missing integer restrictions. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, max 8): variable meaning, correctly translated comparison, valid combined feasible set and boundary/context explanation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Inequality symbol
KeyConcepts.Definition: Symbols <,≤,>,≥ express allowable ranges, with equality included only by ≤ or ≥.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Translate the exact words before solving.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiple constraints
KeyConcepts.Definition: Real-world models can impose a lower and an upper bound at once.

KeyConcepts.Title: Discrete context
KeyConcepts.Definition: Counting people requires whole-number nonnegative solutions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Round limits consistently and check boundaries.

WorkedExamples.Title: Convert a budget statement
WorkedExamples.Question: Write an inequality for $20 fixed fee and $7 per person under at-most $100.
WorkedExamples.Method: Preserve the full system and verify the resulting pair in both original equations.
WorkedExamples.Check: For n=11 total $97, for n=12 total $104.

WorkedExamples.Title: Combine a minimum and maximum
WorkedExamples.Question: At least six participants are needed; what n are feasible?
WorkedExamples.Method: Preserve the full system and verify the resulting pair in both original equations.
Steps: Budget yields n≤80/7, and n must be whole.
Intersect these to obtain integers 6 through 11.
Check n=6 cost $62 and n=11 cost $97.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both participant and cost constraints hold.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distinguish strict from inclusive
WorkedExamples.Question: If a sponsor requires costs strictly below $97 rather than at most $97, is n=11 feasible?
WorkedExamples.Method: Preserve the full system and verify the resulting pair in both original equations.
Steps: Equality does not satisfy a strict < symbol.
The largest whole n below the threshold is 10, cost $90.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No, 11 is excluded; maximum 10 under a strict $97 cap.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A boundary payment at the exact limit is incorrectly excluded.
The algebraic range may contain noninteger counts.

SummaryPoints: Words such as at least, under and no more than determine inequality direction and inclusion.
Budget and participation constraints must be considered together.
For the original example, feasible whole participants are 6–11.
Teacher reviews translation, assumptions and boundary explanations.
